title: Friends that day
hookLine: friends that day will be enemies, except the mindful (43:67)

cards: Two shops on a market street. One sells perfume: walk in, and even if you buy nothing, you leave smelling good, or at least you've breathed something lovely for a few minutes.
Next door, a blacksmith works the bellows: walk in there, and if a spark doesn't burn your clothes, you'll leave smelling of smoke.

The Prophet ﷺ used exactly this picture, recorded in both Bukhari and Muslim, to describe friends. Surah Az-Zukhruf takes the same question, who your friends are, and follows it all the way to the Day.

teach.b: Pickthall: "Friends on that day will be foes one to another, save those who kept their duty (to Allah)." The Arabic for friends is al-akhilla', the plural of khalil.
Not an acquaintance: the closest kind of friend, the one whose love runs through you. Ibrahim is called Khalil Allah, the intimate friend of God.
So the verse means the deepest friendships people have, and it says that on the Day many will turn into enmity. Why?
Commentators explain: friendships built on doing wrong together, on vanity, on using each other, fall apart when everyone sees what they led to. Each friend blames the other.
Another surah gives the voice of such a person: if only I hadn't taken so-and-so as a close friend.
Then the exception: the muttaqin, the mindful, those who kept their duty. Friendships built on goodness don't break that day.
The next verse turns straight to them: O My servants, no fear on you today, and you won't grieve. Words close to these came a few days ago in Fussilat, spoken by angels to those who stand firm.
And the perfume seller comes back. A hadith in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi says a person follows the way of their close friend, so let each of you look at whom you befriend.

teach.h: YOU'LL BE WITH THOSE YOU LOVE.
teach.b: When a man asked the Prophet about someone who loves a group but can't match their deeds, he answered, in Bukhari: a person will be with those they love. Choose your perfume sellers well.

how: Muslims are taught to choose companions who help them toward good, and the hadith of the perfume seller and the blacksmith is often taught to young people about friendship.

o: the closest kind of friend, love that runs deep
a neighbor whose rights come before others
a guest who is owed protection and food

games.q: friends that day — tap the pairs.

s: 43:67 says all friendships end in enmity on the Day
except the mindful: friendships built on goodness last.
it's the closest kind of friend; Ibrahim is called Khalil Allah.
a hadith says a person will be with those they love

games.q: two shops: a perfume seller and a blacksmith. you'll spend an hour in one. according to the Prophet's picture, what's the difference?
o: none, if you don't buy anything.
you leave one smelling good, the other smelling of smoke.
games.why: even without buying, you leave the perfume seller smelling good, and the blacksmith with smoke or a burned sleeve. so with friends.

practice: Bring your closest friends to mind and, for each one, ask gently: when I leave time with them, do I smell of perfume or smoke, am I kinder, more honest, more patient?
Don't judge anyone; just notice, and hold one friend who leaves you better. If you pray, ask that your friendships last beyond this life.

wordCard.voice: Khalil, the closest kind of friend, the bond Az-Zukhruf says breaks into enmity on the Day, except for the mindful. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the closest friends, plural of khalil (43:67).

carryVoice: Your line: friends in goodness last. Perfume or smoke, it stays on you. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Friends on that day will be foes one to another, save those who kept their duty (to Allah).

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5534; Sahih Muslim 2628 (perfume seller and blacksmith)
Sunan Abi Dawud 4833; Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2378 (the way of one's close friend)
